: Resource-to-Skill Construction and Execution-
Guided Skill Evolution for Scientific Computer Use Agents

Daiqiang Li1, Jingyi Peng1, Rui Hu2, Jia Li3, Xuyang Liu4, Guanren Qiao1, Yujia Xiang1, Qiuzhuang Sun5, Zhiping Xu1, Mingrui Luo1,†

1DeepAutonomy Technology Co., Ltd. 2Peking University 3College of AI, Tsinghua University

4The Hong Kong Polytechnic University 5Singapore Management University

 Project Page    Code    Benchmark Environment

11footnotetext: Corresponding author
Abstract

Computer-use agents for scientific software require application-specific expertise. Much of this expertise is already documented in human-authored software manuals and web pages, making them readily available resources for improving agents’ operational capabilities. However, turning these resources into executable, reusable skills remains challenging due to mismatches between documented and deployed software versions and differences in scope between documentation coverage and task requirements. To address these challenges, we introduce ScienceCUA, a two-stage framework combining resource-to-skill construction with execution-guided skill evolution. First, ScienceCUA identifies tasks supported by the software from its documentation, infers operational trajectories, and generalizes them into reusable Skills. Command catalogs, syntax constraints, and shortcuts are organized separately as References for on-demand lookup. Then, ScienceCUA uses execution feedback to drive skill self-evolution by contrasting successful and failed trajectories for the same task, identifying deficiencies, revising existing skills or adding new ones, and updating the skill library only after repeated validation in real environments. To enable reliable evaluation without benchmark noise or task leakage, we introduce two improved benchmarks. ScienceBoard-Verified provides an audited and corrected basis for measuring task performance, while ScienceBoard-VE separates skill evolution from final testing through disjoint evolution and test tasks and further supports native-agent evaluation. Experiments show that the initial Skills and References improve average task success rate by up to 7.23 percentage points over the base model, while skill self-evolution increases the total gain over the baseline to as much as 17.12 percentage points. ScienceCUA turns software documentation into an evolving set of executable skills and queryable references, offering a practical way for general-purpose agents to use scientific software reliably and at scale.

1 Introduction

Computer-use agents (CUAs) built on foundation models can now execute multi-step tasks through graphical and command-line interfaces (Qin et al., 2025; Sager et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2024). Most existing benchmarks, including WebArena, OSWorld, and Windows Agent Arena, focus on general-purpose web, office, and desktop tasks, while scientific software has received comparatively less attention (Xie et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Bonatti et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2026). Scientific software is widely used for experiments, simulations, and data analysis, but operating these tools often requires application-specific workflows, commands, syntax, and parameter constraints (Sun et al., 2026; Ai et al., 2026). To complete scientific-software tasks, agents must use software-specific knowledge to select appropriate operations and organize them into effective workflows (Shao et al., 2026).

We study this problem using ScienceBoard (Sun et al., 2026), which evaluates CUAs on six scientific applications. Figure 2(a) shows that each application provides user manuals or official tutorials containing application-specific knowledge. However, Figure 2(d) shows that directly placing these resources in the model context yields only limited gains in task success while substantially increasing execution time. Figure 2(b) illustrates that human-authored documentation mixes operational instructions with conceptual explanations and other narrative content. A particular task, however, typically depends on only a small fraction of the available information, as shown in Figure 2(c). The central question is how to extract task-relevant information from these human-oriented resources and organize it as structured knowledge that the model can use effectively.

Prior work has constructed reusable skills from human-created resources for content creation, gaming, software operation, and related applications (Fan et al., 2026; Che et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026). For scientific software, these resources must supply two kinds of knowledge with different lifetimes: procedural guidance for a specific task, and shared software knowledge queried on demand. We therefore introduce ScienceCUA, which extracts task-oriented procedural knowledge and cross-task shared software knowledge from raw software resources, organizes them as Skills and References, respectively, and combines them on demand during execution.

However, the initial Skills and References constructed from raw resources have inherent limitations. First, the available PDF or HTML resources may not match the version of the software deployed in the execution environment, since perfectly matched resources are not always available. Second, for some applications, the resource coverage is broader than the range of tasks being evaluated, while the task scope is unknown during construction. The resulting knowledge library therefore contains many entries that are irrelevant to the evaluation tasks, reducing the density of useful information. Third, some task requirements may fall outside the coverage of the resources themselves.

To address these limitations, ScienceCUA drives the continual evolution of Skills and References through execution feedback. Prior work has used task feedback and execution trajectories to build reflective memory, optimize external skills, or adapt agent behavior (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Ni et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2025). In contrast, ScienceCUA improves a scientific-software knowledge library initialized from software resources, using historical failure trajectories to guide subsequent exploration and help agents avoid repeating failed paths or continuing to follow potentially erroneous Skills and References; when knowledge is insufficient, it revisits the original resources to retrieve and construct task-relevant Skills or References. Combined with on-demand composition, this design both helps agents bypass ineffective paths caused by version mismatch and, where the original resources support it, supplements omitted or overly general knowledge in the initial library, thereby reducing the mismatch between the resources and the actual tasks. Candidate updates are added only after independent validation in the target environment.

To support reliable evaluation, we audit and repair ScienceBoard to create ScienceBoard-Verified. We also add a set of tasks that do not overlap with the final test tasks, use them exclusively for skill evolution, and combine the audited benchmark and the new tasks into ScienceBoard-VE; in addition, we extend the evaluation framework to support native agents. Across six scientific applications, the initial Skills and References improve the average task success rate over the base model by up to 7.23 percentage points. Execution-guided skill evolution increases the total gain over the baseline to as much as 17.12 percentage points. Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    Resource-to-skill construction for scientific software. We present a method for constructing a knowledge library from raw software resources. It organizes task-oriented procedural knowledge as Skills and cross-task shared software knowledge as References, and supports their on-demand composition during execution.

  2. 2.

    Execution-feedback-driven skill evolution. We use failure trajectories to guide exploration and help agents avoid repeatedly following erroneous Skills or References. When knowledge is missing or an existing entry is inapplicable, the system supplements or revises Skills and References from the original resources and updates the knowledge library only after validation in the target environment.

  3. 3.

    Reliable evaluation of skill construction and evolution. We audit and repair ScienceBoard to create ScienceBoard-Verified, add skill-evolution tasks disjoint from the final test set to form ScienceBoard-VE, and extend evaluation to native agents.

2 Related Work

Resource-to-Skill Learning.

Automatically constructing reusable agent knowledge from external resources is a relatively recent research direction. MMG2Skill Che et al. (2026) converts public guides into editable Skills, but assumes that tasks are paired with relevant guides in advance and does not realize an end-to-end pipeline for constructing Skills directly from raw resources. VisualSkill Jiang et al. (2026) leverages document images to support GUI element identification and state verification. However, some HTML documentation contains no images and thus provides no additional visual evidence; even when screenshots are available, their interfaces may differ from the current software version, potentially introducing misleading visual cues. SkillFoundry Shen et al. (2026) supports workflow generation for concrete scientific tasks, but focuses on domain capability coverage and task workflows rather than on systematically organizing reusable knowledge for a given scientific software package. Overall, existing methods differ in their resource formats, task assumptions, and construction objectives, but systematic investigation is still lacking into how to automatically discover tasks from raw scientific-software resources and organize cross-task reusable knowledge without pre-specified task–resource pairs.

Self-Evolving Skills and Experience-Driven Agent Adaptation.

Skill self-evolution improves reusable agent knowledge from execution experience without modifying model parameters. Early work such as Reflexion Shinn et al. (2023) used verbal feedback to improve subsequent behavior, and SEAgent Sun et al. (2025) extended this experience-driven paradigm to computer-use agents. Later work made such experience explicit and reusable as skills. EvoSkill Alzubi et al. (2026) creates or revises skills from failure feedback and selects candidates through validation, while Trace2Skill Ni et al. (2026) distills trajectory-local lessons into transferable skill catalogs. As skill updates become central, subsequent studies increasingly focus on their reliability. SkillOpt Yang et al. (2026) constrains the scope of skill edits and accepts only validation-improving updates, while SkillCAT Chen et al. (2026) contrasts successful and failed trajectories for the same task and uses task replay before merging candidate edits. Most prior methods start from execution experience or an existing skill library. ScienceCUA instead initializes its library from scientific-software documentation and addresses version and task-coverage mismatch through failure-history-guided exploration and source-grounded additions or revisions.

3 Method

3.1 Resource-to-Skill Construction

ScienceCUA first transforms software documentation into an initial library of reusable Skills and queryable References, and then evolves this library using execution feedback from a disjoint set of evolution tasks.

Decoupling Skills and References

Given PDF/HTML software documentation 𝒟\mathcal{D}, we construct an initial library ℒ0=(𝒮0,ℛ0)\mathcal{L}_{0}=(\mathcal{S}_{0},\mathcal{R}_{0}), where Skills 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0} encode reusable task-level operational procedures and References ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0} organize cross-task shared knowledge, such as commands, syntax, and parameter constraints. For example, KAlgebra’s 2D and 3D plotting workflows form separate Skills, while syntax for square roots and exponentiation is stored in a Reference (Figure 3). During execution, the agent selects a Skill for the required workflow and consults References as needed to incorporate software knowledge into its actions.

Construction Pipeline

We represent a Skill as s=(ns,ds,as,ps,bs)s=(n_{s},d_{s},a_{s},p_{s},b_{s}), where nsn_{s} is its name, dsd_{s} is its capability description, asa_{s} specifies its applicability, psp_{s} lists its preconditions, and bsb_{s} contains its procedural body, including the steps needed to accomplish the goal. We represent a Reference as r=(nr,dr,cr)r=(n_{r},d_{r},c_{r}), where nrn_{r} is its name, drd_{r} describes its purpose, and crc_{r} contains the concrete lookup content. Construction first organizes the documentation into a shared evidence corpus. From this corpus, one branch extracts References, while the other discovers Tasks, infers trajectories, and induces Skills.

Traceable evidence organization.

To support all downstream stages and reduce hallucinations, we organize documentation into traceable evidence. A parser uses authored headings and navigation to structure text and visual content while retaining source locations. An agent refines this organization without rewriting the content. Every downstream Reference, Task, and inferred action or observation must be grounded in this evidence.

Reference extraction.

To make shared software knowledge accessible during execution, the Reference branch turns relevant evidence into focused lookup entries. A program first extracts and deduplicates candidate lookup content from the documentation, including command tables, syntax constraints, and shortcut descriptions. An agent reviews the remaining candidates to decide what to retain and how to group them, preserving documented syntax, parameters, and examples.

Task discovery, trajectory inference, and Skill induction.

To ground reusable Skills in concrete operational requirements, the other branch proceeds from goals to trajectories before induction. An agent first discovers source-supported user goals without benchmark task input. For each Task, it infers ordered actions and expected observations, retaining documented controls. These trajectories make the required operations explicit before related procedures are grouped into a coherent Skill, helping preserve actionable detail during abstraction. After induction, we check whether the operational capability expressed by each trajectory is included in a Skill and explicitly record any exclusions.

Each stage produces structured outputs that serve as inputs to subsequent stages, yielding the initial library ℒ0=(𝒮0,ℛ0)\mathcal{L}_{0}=(\mathcal{S}_{0},\mathcal{R}_{0}). Reference extraction, Task discovery, trajectory inference, and Skill induction are assigned to independent agents, each with its own tools, prompt, and required output format. A unified description of the Resource-to-Skill pipeline, including agent roles and tools, prompts, and output schemas, is provided in Appendix F.

3.2 Execution-Guided Skill Self-Evolution

Differences between documented and deployed software versions, together with gaps between resource coverage and task requirements, can leave the initial library misaligned with the target environment or incomplete for its tasks. ScienceCUA therefore keeps the execution model fixed and continually evolves Skills and References through two mechanisms: failure-history-guided exploration and source-grounded knowledge addition.

Evolution setting and overall workflow.

As described in Section 4.2, ScienceBoard-VE contains an evolution set E=Expanded∖VerifiedE=\mathrm{Expanded}\setminus\mathrm{Verified} and a held-out test set V=VerifiedV=\mathrm{Verified}, where E∩V=∅E\cap V=\emptyset. Evolution uses EE, while VV remains unseen until final evaluation. Given the initial library ℒ0=(𝒮0,ℛ0)\mathcal{L}_{0}=(\mathcal{S}_{0},\mathcal{R}_{0}), ScienceCUA processes each task q∈Eq\in E independently and maintains its history ℋq\mathcal{H}_{q}. Histories and provisional updates are not shared across tasks.

Each task uses two types of execution. Task exploration attempts the task with the frozen initial library, together with any prior failure records available, to search for a feasible path and collect environmental feedback. Candidate validation temporarily loads one modified or newly added Skill or Reference and reruns the task to test whether that candidate can independently support successful execution.

Each task begins with task exploration. A first-exploration success requires no update and exits the evolution process. After a failure, the system either makes no change, revises existing knowledge, or adds source-supported knowledge according to its diagnosis. Any modified or newly added Skill or Reference undergoes candidate validation. A successful candidate enters the candidate pool 𝒫\mathcal{P}. A failed candidate and its validation trajectory enter ℋq\mathcal{H}_{q} to guide the next task exploration. If a later exploration succeeds with the help of failure history, the system contrasts it with earlier failures, derives a revision candidate when needed, and validates it. Each task contributes at most one validated candidate to 𝒫\mathcal{P}. These candidates are then consolidated into ℒfinal\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{final}}, merged targets undergo regression certification, and the library is frozen for evaluation. Further details are provided in Appendix I.

Failure-history-guided exploration.

The first exploration of task qq performs normal routing over ℒ0\mathcal{L}_{0} by selecting entries from their names and descriptions; the routed Skills and References define ℱq⊆ℒ0\mathcal{F}_{q}\subseteq\mathcal{L}_{0}. Later task explorations load the same entries in their initial versions and additionally receive the accumulated failure history. Formally, the ii-th exploration is τq(i)=Executeθ⁡(q,ℒ0,ℱq,ℋq(i))\tau_{q}^{(i)}=\operatorname{Execute}_{\theta}(q;\mathcal{L}_{0},\mathcal{F}_{q},\mathcal{H}_{q}^{(i)}), where ℋq(1)=∅\mathcal{H}_{q}^{(1)}=\emptyset. For i>1i>1, ℋq(i)\mathcal{H}_{q}^{(i)} contains the task’s earlier failed task explorations and candidate validations, including their trajectories, screenshots, and outcomes. These failure records help the model avoid paths that failed because of version mismatch, rather than mechanically follow initial knowledge that conflicts with the deployed software. Later explorations always start from the same ℒ0\mathcal{L}_{0} and ℱq\mathcal{F}_{q}: failure history changes exploration behavior, whereas knowledge changes still require independent validation. Appendix I.2 specifies the archived evidence and its input format.

Failure diagnosis and candidate construction.

For a failed task exploration, the diagnosis module analyzes its loaded Skills and References, trajectory, screenshots, and evaluator outcome, and assigns one primary cause: (1) grounding failure, where interface perception or manipulation is the main obstacle and no candidate is produced; (2) modify existing knowledge, where one entry in ℱq\mathcal{F}_{q} is relevant but contains an incorrect or incomplete procedure, condition, parameter, or version-dependent instruction; or (3) add new knowledge, where the routed knowledge has a genuine coverage gap and triggers retrieval from the original resources 𝒟\mathcal{D}. The modify branch produces one complete revision candidate Δq(i)\Delta_{q}^{(i)}; the add branch produces a new Skill or Reference candidate only when retrieval finds sufficient source support. Any resulting candidate is independently validated: success adds it to 𝒫\mathcal{P} and terminates task qq, whereas failure records it in ℋq\mathcal{H}_{q} before task exploration resumes. Separately, only when a later task exploration itself succeeds does the system contrast that success with earlier failures and either revise one entry in ℱq\mathcal{F}_{q} or make no change; this branch cannot add knowledge. Details are provided in Appendices I.3 and I.4.

Independent candidate validation.

For candidate Δq(i)\Delta_{q}^{(i)}, ScienceCUA constructs the temporary library ℒ~q(i)=ℒ0⊕Δq(i)\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{q}^{(i)}=\mathcal{L}_{0}\oplus\Delta_{q}^{(i)}, where ⊕\oplus replaces one initial entry with its revision or inserts one source-supported new entry. Validation then executes τ~q(i)=Executeθ⁡(q,ℒ~q(i),ℱ~q(i),∅)\widetilde{\tau}_{q}^{(i)}=\operatorname{Execute}_{\theta}(q;\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{q}^{(i)},\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}_{q}^{(i)},\emptyset) in a reset environment and a fresh session. It fixes the route obtained by the first task exploration, with the candidate entry substituted or added, and receives no prior trajectory, diagnosis, or candidate rationale, thereby testing whether the candidate knowledge itself supports the task. A successful candidate enters 𝒫\mathcal{P}; a failed candidate remains inactive, and its execution record is added to the task’s failure history. Appendix I.3 gives the complete validation protocol.

4 ScienceBoard-VE: A Verified and Expanded Benchmark for Scientific Computer-Use Agents

ScienceBoard (Sun et al., 2026) is a benchmark for scientific computer-use agents and has been adopted in subsequent studies on agent evaluation, training, and task expansion (Lv et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). During reproduction, we audited all 169 original tasks and identified issues in task instructions, task statements, reference answers, evaluators, and execution environments. We therefore construct ScienceBoard-Verified and add a disjoint set of tasks for skill self-evolution. Together, they form ScienceBoard-VE. We also extend the evaluation framework to support native-agent evaluation. Figure 4 summarizes the task distribution and benchmark quality assurance.

4.1 ScienceBoard-Verified

We substantively revise 37 tasks and remove one additional task, yielding 168 executable tasks reserved for final evaluation. We organize the revisions and supporting repairs into four categories: (1) Instruction Ambiguity, which covers 15 revised tasks with unclear goals or omitted completion requirements; (2) Task & Answer Errors, which covers 12 revised tasks involving incorrect task statements, reference answers, or expected evaluator results; (3) Evaluator Bias, which covers 10 revised tasks in which unnecessary restrictions exclude valid execution paths, output representations, or output locations; and (4) Environment Repairs, which covers application prompts, response handling, runtime and initialization settings, and unavailable external dependencies. The fourth category includes shared evaluation-environment repairs and the removed task; these do not add to the 37 revised tasks. Appendix G details all 37 task revisions, the task removal rationale, and the associated evaluation-environment repairs.

4.2 Expanding the Benchmark for Skill Self-Evolution

To separate skill improvement from final evaluation, we add 108 tasks that do not overlap with the verified test set: 20 each for KAlgebra, Celestia, GRASS GIS, ChimeraX, and Lean 4, and 8 for TeXstudio. These tasks are used exclusively for skill self-evolution, while the 168 tasks in ScienceBoard-Verified remain unseen during skill construction and evolution and are used only for final evaluation. The resulting ScienceBoard-VE contains 276 executable tasks in total. The evolution tasks use the same types of software operations as the test tasks but differ in their specific targets or requirements, allowing execution experience to transfer without reusing the test tasks themselves. See Appendix H for details.

4.3 Native-Agent Evaluation

The original ScienceBoard evaluates models through a unified API-based interaction loop. We extend it to support native evaluation of Codex and Grok Build, keeping tasks, software environments, and evaluators unchanged. In both settings, ScienceBoard supplies screenshots and accessibility trees, executes the returned action code or control instructions, and evaluates task outcomes. In the model-based setting, each API request includes the system prompt, task instruction, screenshots and accessibility trees from the three most recent steps together with the model-generated actions for those steps, and the current screenshot and accessibility tree. For ScienceCUA, we implement two-stage resource routing through progressive disclosure. Before execution, the evaluated model selects relevant Skills and References from their names and descriptions based on the task instruction. The selected entries are then loaded in full into the system prompt and included in every subsequent execution request. In the native-agent setting, each task uses a separate persistent session, to which the outer evaluation framework appends only the current screenshot and accessibility tree at each step. The native harness maintains the task history and compacts context as needed. Skills and References are registered as independently loadable native resources, which the agent selects and reads during execution. Each turn concludes with one ScienceBoard action block for the evaluation framework to execute. To prevent agents from obtaining additional reference material through web search, we disable web search for native agents. To preserve task independence, conversation history and runtime context are maintained separately for each task and are not shared between tasks.

5 Experiments

Experimental setup.

We evaluate ScienceCUA on ScienceBoard-Verified. Model-based evaluation uses Qwen-3.8 Max, GLM-5.2, Grok-4.6, and GPT-5.5. Native-agent evaluation uses Grok Build with Grok-4.6 and Codex with GPT-5.5. The two settings follow the respective interaction and resource access protocols described in Section 4.3. In model-based ScienceCUA evaluation, at most three Skill and Reference entries are selected in total before each task. In native-agent evaluation, the agent autonomously selects and reads resources during execution, with no limit on the number of Skill and Reference entries it can access. We report task success rates for each of the six applications and use their unweighted mean as the overall performance metric.

Model-based evaluation compares ScienceCUA with Vanilla, direct document injection, RAG, VisualSkill, and SkillFoundry. Native-agent evaluation compares Vanilla, VisualSkill, SkillFoundry, and ScienceCUA. ScienceCUA and VisualSkill use the same documentation inputs. SkillFoundry does not support direct documentation input and instead automatically searches for and collects online resources based on the name and version of the software installed in the execution environment. Implementation details are provided in Appendix B for direct injection, Appendix C for RAG, Appendix D for SkillFoundry, and Appendix E for VisualSkill.

Skill self-evolution uses the 108 additional tasks in ScienceBoard-VE. After evolution, the knowledge library is frozen and evaluated on ScienceBoard-Verified without access to evolution trajectories or histories.

5.1 RQ1: Can ScienceCUA-constructed resources improve task success in scientific software operation?

Table 1 shows that the initial ScienceCUA library achieves the highest average success rate in all four model-based settings. ScienceCUA improves over Vanilla by 5.76–7.23 percentage points, compared with 1.53–3.42 points for direct document injection, and outperforms RAG, VisualSkill, and SkillFoundry across all four models. The gains also extend to native-agent evaluation. ScienceCUA reaches average success rates of 55.41% with Grok Build and 59.82% with Codex, improving over their respective Vanilla baselines by 9.12 and 5.73 percentage points and outperforming VisualSkill and SkillFoundry in both settings. Figure 5(a) shows that ScienceCUA requires 21.1–28.9% less total task execution time than direct document injection across the four models. ScienceCUA also reduces total initial library construction time by 62.2% and 34.6% relative to VisualSkill and SkillFoundry, respectively (Figure 5(b)). These results support the usefulness of the constructed Skills and References as initial operational knowledge for scientific software.

5.2 RQ2: Do Skills and References make complementary contributions to task success?

We ablate Skills and References separately to assess the individual and joint contributions of procedural guidance and cross-task shared lookup knowledge to task success. Skills organize complete operational procedures around specific goals, while References provide shared knowledge that is not tied to any single procedure, including syntax constraints, parameter rules, command and function catalogs, and keyboard shortcuts. The two resource types have no one-to-one correspondence that permits direct, equivalent merging. We therefore do not use a forced merger of the two resource types as an information-matched control for knowledge organization, and instead use resource ablations to evaluate the value of providing each knowledge type individually and both jointly.

Table 2 shows that providing either resource type alone improves average success rates over Vanilla, while providing both achieves the best results. In model-based evaluation with Grok-4.6, the average success rates are 40.09% with Skills alone, 40.62% with References alone, and 44.70% with both. The corresponding results for native Grok Build are 49.89%, 51.14%, and 55.41%. The relative gains from the two resource types vary across applications, while providing both further improves overall performance, supporting the complementary contributions of procedural guidance and shared lookup knowledge to task execution.

The KAlgebra C-05 comparison in Appendix J illustrates these roles under the same budget of five interaction turns. Each condition retains autonomous routing over the permitted resource types. Reference-only spends its budget locating the script-loading interface; Skill-only loads the script but leaves the calculation symbolic. With both types, the agent combines the script-loading Skill’s guidance with application-specific knowledge from the function-catalog Reference, then corrects an intermediate vector-valued result using execution feedback to complete the task.

Figure 5(c) further illustrates actual calls to both resource types during task execution. Native Grok Build with Grok-4.6 (xhigh) accesses at least one resource in 156 of the 168 tasks (92.9%). Final task attempts contain 291 completed Skill calls and 543 completed Reference calls, with repeated calls to the same entry counted separately. These records show that the agent calls both Skills and References during actual task execution and, together with the preceding ablation results, support the contributions of both knowledge types to task completion.

5.3 RQ3: Can self-evolution mitigate the limitations of Resource-to-Skill construction?

The initial library may lack task-relevant knowledge or contain instructions incompatible with the deployed software version. We use Grok-4.6 (xhigh) and GPT-5.5 (xhigh) to compare the initial library, Full ScienceCUA, two ablated variants, Trace2Skill (Ni et al., 2026), and SkillCAT (Chen et al., 2026), examining whether execution-guided self-evolution improves performance on unseen tasks. The −-Knowledge addition variant only revises existing entries without adding new Skills or References. The −-Failure history variant withholds prior exploration and candidate-validation records from subsequent exploration, leaving the other mechanisms unchanged. Within each model setting, all evolution variants use the same initial library, evolution tasks, software environments, and runtime configurations. Detailed ScienceCUA settings are provided in Appendix I.

Table 3 shows that self-evolution improves the average success rate from 44.70% to 54.59% for Grok-4.6 and from 57.16% to 65.81% for GPT-5.5, yielding gains of 9.89 and 8.65 percentage points, respectively. Full ScienceCUA also outperforms Trace2Skill and SkillCAT, which achieve average success rates of 46.44% and 53.02% with Grok-4.6, and 60.46% and 63.74% with GPT-5.5, respectively. These results indicate that knowledge improvements obtained during evolution transfer to final test tasks not used during evolution.

Removing either knowledge addition or failure history reduces average success rates, but the dominant source of improvement varies by application. KAlgebra and Celestia are particularly sensitive to failure history: removing it reduces success by 9.68 percentage points for KAlgebra under both models, and by 9.09 and 6.06 points for Celestia under Grok-4.6 and GPT-5.5, respectively. Documentation-version mismatches leave some initial entries with inapplicable capability constraints or interface paths. Appendix K traces how execution feedback repairs such a constraint in KAlgebra, while Appendix M shows how outdated interface guidance consumes execution steps in an initial Celestia run. GRASS GIS benefits especially from knowledge addition: removing it reduces success by 14.71 and 5.89 points under the two models. Its broad documentation leaves task-relevant module options underspecified in the initial library; Appendix L shows how adding a module-level Reference fills this gap and supports related Verified tasks. Gains are smaller or less consistent for the other applications. Lean 4 tasks require specialized formal proofs that the general theorem-proving guide rarely supplies directly, while many TeXstudio tasks require information from other software beyond the TeXstudio manual. Appendix N compares these task requirements with the source documentation.

6 Conclusion

We present ScienceCUA, a two-stage framework for computer-use agents operating scientific software. The first stage extracts source-grounded operational knowledge from software documentation, distilling task-level workflows into executable Skills and organizing commands, syntax, and parameter constraints as queryable References. The second stage refines Skills and References using execution feedback from the target software environment. We also construct the audited ScienceBoard-Verified and add evolution tasks disjoint from the test set to form ScienceBoard-VE, supporting knowledge evolution and native-agent evaluation. Experiments across six scientific applications show that the initial Skills and References improve average task success by up to 7.23 percentage points over the baseline in model-based evaluation. Knowledge self-evolution increases the total gain to as much as 17.12 percentage points. These results suggest that human-authored software resources can be transformed into executable, verifiable operational knowledge that continually improves through environmental feedback, enhancing general-purpose agents’ ability to use scientific software. By maintaining Skills and References outside the model parameters, ScienceCUA offers a practical path for agents to adapt to changes in scientific software environments and task requirements without retraining the model.
