Appendix A Discussion and Implications

Niche and private software are priority settings for our approach.

Knowledge of niche, private, or self-developed software may be underrepresented during general models’ pre-training and post-training, leaving gaps in their understanding of specific functions, workflows, and usage constraints. Extracting knowledge from documentation therefore has the potential to yield larger performance gains for such software. Execution feedback can then guide revisions and additions that adapt this knowledge to the deployed environment and task requirements. For widely used software whose operational knowledge is well covered during training, models may already know much of the documented material, leaving less room for improvement through external knowledge.

Knowledge organization should reflect software and task requirements.

Scientific software requires both operational workflows and precise parameter constraints, syntax rules, and command and function catalogs. These details are often shared across tasks and consulted only when a step requires them. ScienceCUA therefore organizes goal-oriented procedural knowledge as Skills and shared lookup knowledge as References, allowing agents to follow workflows while accessing specific rules and details on demand. Other software and scenarios may require different forms of knowledge organization. Applying our approach to these settings can retain the process of constructing knowledge from resources and improving it through execution, while adapting knowledge organization to the target setting. Such adaptation could include exploring code-based or visual representations, whose effectiveness we have not systematically compared within the same framework.

Base model capabilities affect the value of external knowledge augmentation.

Recent frontier models, such as GPT-6 Astra, demonstrate stronger computer-use capabilities. As models become able to complete more scientific-software tasks on their own, the additional gains from ScienceCUA’s self-evolved Skills and References may diminish, a pattern observed in our supplementary experiments (Appendix P). Similar effects may arise in other CUA settings: when a base model already possesses the relevant operational knowledge, the room for improvement from Skills may shrink; if their guidance is outdated, inapplicable to the task, or imposes unnecessary constraints on execution paths, it may even interfere with the model’s own judgment and lead to worse performance than the base model without Skills. The value of external knowledge therefore needs to be evaluated in relation to the base model’s capabilities and the specific task. Practical deployment must also balance task performance against inference cost. In budget-constrained settings that call for lower-cost models, constructing and continually improving external knowledge from software resources retains practical value. Moreover, the software covered by ScienceBoard has publicly available documentation, and models may already have learned some of this operational knowledge. For niche, private, or self-developed software whose knowledge is underrepresented during model training, external knowledge may still fill capability gaps and yield larger gains. This expectation warrants further empirical validation.

Appendix B Direct Documentation Injection Details

Direct injection follows the model-based evaluation protocol in Section 4.3. Each API request includes the system prompt, task instruction, screenshots and accessibility trees from the three most recent steps together with the model-generated actions for those steps, and the current screenshot and accessibility tree. Documentation for the corresponding application is added to every request. ScienceBoard executes the action code or control instructions returned by the model.

Direct injection is constrained by the model’s context window. Table 4 lists the officially documented context limits of the four evaluated models. These windows must accommodate documentation, task instructions, interaction history, and other inputs while leaving room for model output; they cannot be allocated entirely to documentation.

Model Context window Official source
Qwen-3.8 Max 1M tokens Qwen documentation
GLM-5.2 1M tokens Z.AI documentation
Grok-4.6 500,000 tokens Grok model documentation
GPT-5.5 1,050,000 tokens OpenAI model documentation

The complete documentation for some applications also contains substantial amounts of text, requiring considerable context space for full injection. As shown in Table 5, the full GRASS GIS and ChimeraX documentation contains approximately 12.2 million and 1.7 million text characters, respectively. Injecting these materials in full at every step, alongside task and interaction inputs, creates a risk of exceeding the context window.

Software Format
Full documentation
(characters)
Selected documentation
(characters)
KAlgebra PDF 27,572 27,572
Celestia PDF 146,761 146,761
GRASS GIS HTML 12,232,449 367,177
ChimeraX HTML 1,704,478 254,697
Lean 4 HTML 527,662 527,662
TeXstudio HTML 243,645 243,645

Full documentation refers to all materials within the documentation scope specified in this work. Both columns use the same character-counting procedure: text is extracted from PDF text layers or HTML with tags removed, whitespace is normalized, and characters are counted including whitespace. Navigation text is retained for HTML.

Given these context limits and documentation sizes, we use a fixed documentation configuration for each application. KAlgebra and Celestia receive their complete original PDF files. For Lean 4 and TeXstudio, we acquire all pages within the specified documentation scope and inject their normalized text in full. For GRASS GIS and ChimeraX, we use bounded page acquisition: the root page is retained, and 40 child pages are selected in traversal-depth order with round-robin scheduling across root-level chapter branches. The normalized text of all selected pages is then injected in full. All documentation is fixed before evaluation, shared across tasks and evaluated models for the same application, and included in full in every execution request, without task-specific retrieval or dynamic selection during execution.

Appendix C Retrieval-Augmented Generation Details

This appendix describes the retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. Offline preprocessing freezes one corpus per application, applies structure-preserving chunking and hybrid retrieval, and materializes task-specific context bundles for deterministic loading at execution. All tasks of an application share the same corpus. Documents are never manually paired with tasks.

C.1 Frozen Documentation Corpora

We construct one physically isolated corpus for each of the six applications. Table 6 reports its documentation input and size. Raw inputs, normalized text, source locators, acquisition records, and manifests are all frozen before retrieval. Bundle generation and benchmark execution use only these local snapshots, shared across all tasks and evaluated models for an application.

Software Environment Format Frozen documentation source Pages Documents Chunks
KAlgebra 24.11.70 PDF KAlgebra Handbook 32 88 96
Celestia 1.7.0 PDF Celestia 1.6.1 User’s Guide 48 48 57
GRASS GIS 8.4.1 HTML GRASS GIS 8.4.1 Reference Manual 1,468 11,444 24,236
ChimeraX 1.9 HTML UCSF ChimeraX online User Guide, frozen at acquisition 277 726 859
Lean 4 4.14.0 HTML Theorem Proving in Lean 4, version 4.26.0 13 113 146
TeXstudio 4.8.6 HTML TeXstudio 4.9.8 documentation 9 269 294
Total 1,847 12,688 25,688
PDF normalization.

PDF text is extracted with PyMuPDF from the embedded text layer. OCR is disabled and raster images are not indexed. Repeated headers and footers are removed. We infer a hierarchy from chapter, section, appendix, and numbered headings and retain page ranges as source locators. When a reliable semantic heading is unavailable, the corresponding page is kept as a page-level document rather than discarded. This yields 81 semantic sections and 7 page fallbacks for KAlgebra. The Celestia guide is retained as 48 page-level documents because its layout does not provide sufficiently reliable semantic section boundaries.

HTML acquisition and freezing.

Each HTML corpus begins at a fixed official documentation root. URLs are canonicalized and restricted to the documentation scope. The reachable in-scope link queue is traversed to exhaustion, with no page-count limit, and every successful response is frozen with its requested URL, final URL, acquisition time, raw HTML hash, outgoing links, and local file locator. GRASS GIS contains 1,468 successful pages and ChimeraX contains 277. Both acquisition queues have zero pending URLs. Images, video, CSS, JavaScript, PDFs, and pages outside the documentation scope are excluded. The Lean 4 and TeXstudio documentation trees contain 13 and 9 in-scope pages, respectively, all of which are retained.

HTML normalization.

For every retained page, the extractor selects the main, article, or body content and removes scripts, styles, templates, and navigation chrome. It segments the remaining content at h1–h6 boundaries. Paragraphs, lists, tables, and preformatted code are preserved in reading order, with code represented as fenced blocks. Exact duplicate pages are removed by content hash. Raw HTML and normalized Markdown-compatible text are both retained for audit, but only normalized text is indexed. This procedure is deterministic and uses no language model.

C.2 Structure-Preserving Chunking

Chunk boundaries are computed with the tokenizer of BAAI/bge-m3. Each indexable text is prefixed with its document title and complete section breadcrumb. The target length is 700 tokens and the hard maximum, including this prefix, is 1,000 tokens. Text that exceeds the limit is split preferentially at paragraph, line, or sentence boundaries with an 80-token overlap between consecutive pieces. Chunks never cross documents or semantic sections. Exact duplicates are removed using the SHA-256 hash of the complete index text. Near-duplicate removal is not applied. The counts in Table 6 are post-deduplication, and no resulting chunk exceeds the hard limit.

C.3 Hybrid Retrieval and Reranking

Retrieval is performed independently for each application. The query is exactly the stripped task instruction. The software name is used only to select the corresponding corpus and is not appended to the query. Cross-application retrieval is disabled.

We retrieve 30 candidates with BM25 and 30 with a dense encoder. BM25 uses k1=1.2k_{1}=1.2, b=0.75b=0.75, binary query term frequency, and a Unicode-aware tokenizer that preserves compound identifiers. Dense retrieval uses BAAI/bge-m3 with a maximum input length of 1,024 tokens, CLS pooling, and L2-normalized embeddings. Encoding uses FP16 on CUDA with batch size 2. The resulting 1,024-dimensional vectors are stored in FP32. Similarity is exact cosine similarity, implemented as a dot product over normalized vectors, without approximate-nearest-neighbor search.

The two ranked lists are combined by equal-weight reciprocal rank fusion (RRF):

RRF⁡(d)=∑s∈{BM25,dense}160+ranks⁡(d).\operatorname{RRF}(d)=\sum_{s\in\{\mathrm{BM25},\mathrm{dense}\}}\frac{1}{60+\operatorname{rank}_{s}(d)}. (1)

The 40 highest-scoring fused candidates are reranked with BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3. The reranker uses a maximum input length of 1,024 tokens, FP16 CUDA inference, batch size 4, and its unnormalized output score. Ties are resolved deterministically using the fused score and chunk identifier.

We select up to five reranked chunks whose rendered references fit a 6,000-token context budget. Each numbered reference gives its rank, document title, section breadcrumb, and chunk text. Retrieval scores are hidden. The references are enclosed by documentation markers and prepended to the unmodified original task instruction.

C.4 Frozen Task Bundles and Runtime Protocol

Offline retrieval produces one frozen bundle per ScienceBoard-Verified task, storing the query, corpus and index identities, configuration hash, candidate rankings, final five chunks, and rendered instruction. The 168 bundles comprise 31 for KAlgebra, 33 for Celestia, 34 for GRASS GIS, 28 for ChimeraX, 26 for Lean 4, and 16 for TeXstudio. Each is reused across all evaluated models.

At initialization, hashes and identities are verified. Invalid bundles fail without live fallback. Runtime uses no retrieval assets or evaluation data.

Appendix D SkillFoundry Reproduction Details

This appendix describes our reproduction of SkillFoundry as a Resource-to-Skill baseline.

D.1 Reproduction Setup

We reproduced the complete SkillFoundry pipeline from an empty repository state, without an external taxonomy or any pre-existing resource or skill library. Each target software package was processed in an isolated repository, and no task list or task-specific resource pairing was provided. Under this setting, SkillFoundry was responsible for constructing the software-specific taxonomy, discovering supporting resources, and building reusable skills from the retrieved evidence.

Software Environment version
KAlgebra 24.11.70
Celestia 1.7.0
GRASS GIS 8.4.1
Lean 4 4.14.0
TeXstudio 4.8.6
ChimeraX 1.9

D.2 Inputs and Configuration

Each run received only the software name and environment version. Table 7 lists the six targets used in our experiments. We used the same execution configuration for all targets: stage-workers=1, background-validation-limit=0, and verification-mode=standard.

D.3 Reproduction Procedure

For each target, we executed one complete five-stage cycle in the standard order: tree_check, resource_search, skill_build, skill_test, and refresh. The pipeline first constructed a software-specific capability taxonomy, then searched for and registered relevant external resources. It subsequently synthesized skills from the registered evidence, ran SkillFoundry’s repository-local validation, and synchronized the resulting taxonomy, resource registry, and skill registry. The generated skills were then evaluated on ScienceBoard-Verified using the same downstream protocol as the other Resource-to-Skill methods.

Appendix E VisualSkill Reproduction Details

This appendix describes our reproduction of VisualSkill as a Resource-to-Skill baseline.

E.1 Reproduction Setup

We reproduced VisualSkill’s standard multimodal Stage 1 pipeline rather than its task-filtered mode. Each run processed one target application with exactly one curated documentation source, either a PDF manual or an HTML documentation root. PDF and HTML inputs were not mixed within a run, no external task list was provided for taxonomy filtering, and the optional text-derivation phase was not used.

E.2 Inputs and Configuration

Table 8 lists the documentation source supplied for each target, with public links to the documentation resources.

We used --mode multimodal for all six targets. PDF sources were supplied through sources.pdf_guide.url, whereas HTML sources were supplied through sources.html_guide.root_url; otherwise, the same Stage 1 construction setting was used across targets.

E.3 Reproduction Procedure

For each target, we ran the standard Stage 1 construction pipeline. VisualSkill first built a category–topic taxonomy from the supplied documentation, then prepared topic-level textual and visual evidence from the corresponding PDF pages or HTML pages. It next generated a multimodal guide.md for each topic and produced a use_when routing description. These topic-level artifacts were finally assembled into the top-level SKILL.md. The generated skills were then evaluated on ScienceBoard-Verified using the same downstream protocol as the other Resource-to-Skill methods.

Appendix F Resource-to-Skill Implementation Details

This appendix provides implementation details for the Resource-to-Skill pipeline in Sec. 3.1. The main text focuses on the knowledge-construction logic; here we report the executable child-session contracts and deterministic validation. Lower-level parser corner cases, full tool JSON schemas, retry/error handling, and storage internals are left to the released implementation.

F.1 DSH Child Session Contracts

A DSH child session is defined by more than its prompt. For an Agent aa, the complete executable contract is

ℭa=(Pa,Ia,Ta,Ba,Oa,Va,τa),\mathfrak{C}_{a}=(P_{a},I_{a},T_{a},B_{a},O_{a},V_{a},\tau_{a}), (2)

where PaP_{a} is the prompt, IaI_{a} is the input scope, TaT_{a} is the allowed tool surface, BaB_{a} is the tool budget, OaO_{a} is the structured output contract, VaV_{a} is the Python validator, and τa\tau_{a} is the termination protocol. A child session can observe only authorized objects exposed through TaT_{a} and can modify pipeline state only through the designated structured submission tools.

The HTML and PDF Evidence Architect contracts are source-type-specific and mutually exclusive. The HTML child accepts only one normalized HTML root scope, comprising the root page and all eligible in-scope child pages; the PDF child accepts only one normalized PDF document. Neither child may be dispatched a source of the other type.

F.2 Deterministic Validation and Control

All Agent outputs are validated by Python before entering a downstream stage. A textual citation must contain a quote that exactly matches the corresponding Evidence text; a visual claim must reference an authorized and inspected image artifact. Citations cannot point to nonexistent or out-of-scope Evidence, and downstream objects can reference only upstream identifiers present in the current frozen snapshot.

Stage-specific validation additionally checks schema constraints, duplicate candidates, field lengths, step ordering, and cross-object consistency. For Trajectories, Python verifies that the submitted task_id matches the dispatched Task, that exactly one acceptable trajectory is returned, that step ordinals are consecutive, and that linked References exist and satisfy the reference_guided dependency rules. For Skills, Python validates Task/Trajectory/Reference relations, step structure, exact citations, and the coverage protocol over every dispatched Trajectory.

Pipeline state changes only through structured submission tools. Ordinary natural-language replies do not commit business results. Key stages freeze immutable CorpusSnapshot and KnowledgeSnapshot objects so that downstream child sessions read stable inputs. Attempt/Receipt bookkeeping, idempotent retry, recovery, and storage details are implementation mechanisms and are documented in the released code rather than expanded here.

Appendix G ScienceBoard-Verified: Detailed Repairs

This appendix documents the 37 task revisions and one task removal made when constructing ScienceBoard-Verified, corresponding to the 38 revised or removed tasks summarized in Figure 4. A task may involve multiple issues; we assign it to one category to avoid double counting and describe secondary changes in the same entry. The first three categories contain 15, 12, and 10 revised tasks, respectively. The fourth contains the removed task and shared evaluation-environment repairs, which are not counted as additional task revisions.

G.1 Instruction Ambiguity

These revisions clarify the intended target, information source, or completion requirements so that the instructions explicitly state what the evaluator expects.

1. Celestia A-02: Time direction and rate.

The original instruction, “-20x slower,” could be interpreted as running backward at 20 times normal speed, whereas the evaluator expects a time scale of 0.05. The revised instruction explicitly requests forward playback at 0.05x, or 20 times slower than real time.

2. Celestia C-06: Ambiguous G0 star selection.

The instruction asks for the name of the “only” G0 star, but the software lists multiple stars of this spectral type. We specify the closest G0 star to identify the intended object unambiguously.

3. Celestia C-10: Unspecified distance convention.

Asking for the globular cluster “farthest from the Milky Way” could prompt agents to change the distance reference. The revision instead specifies the cluster with the largest Distance (ly) value in Celestia’s Deep Sky Objects browser and requests its radius in light-years to two decimal places.

4. TeXstudio A-01: Angle insertion.

The task asks the agent to measure an angle between specified atoms in ChimeraX and replace a placeholder in the article. The evaluator checks the saved file and compilation result, but these requirements were omitted from the instruction. We explicitly require saving the TeX file and ensuring successful compilation.

5. TeXstudio A-02: Residue-name insertion.

The task asks for the name of residue /A:6 to be inserted into a table. We add the previously unstated requirements to save the TeX file and ensure that it compiles successfully.

6. TeXstudio A-03: DNA sequence correction.

The task asks the agent to correct the Chain A DNA sequence using ChimeraX. We explicitly require saving the corrected TeX file and successful compilation, matching the conditions checked by the evaluator.

7. TeXstudio A-04: Fibonacci value correction.

The task asks the agent to obtain the Fibonacci value f⁡(24)f(24) in KAlgebra and replace an incorrect value in the article. The revision adds saving and successful compilation as explicit completion requirements.

8. TeXstudio B-01: Lean 4 citation.

The task asks the agent to fill a citation in main.tex using the existing Lean 4 entry in refs.bib, without modifying the bibliography file. We preserve these constraints and add the requirements to save the TeX file and ensure successful compilation.

9. TeXstudio B-02: COSPAR identifier and citation.

The task asks for Gemini 9A’s COSPAR identifier followed immediately by a Celestia citation. We clarify that the completed TeX file must be saved and compile successfully.

10. TeXstudio B-03: Province count and citation.

The task asks the agent to insert the number of provinces in Piemonte and a GRASS GIS citation into the article. We add the missing requirements to save the TeX file and ensure successful compilation.

11. TeXstudio C-01: Atom-count correction.

The task asks the agent to correct a C, O, or N atom count using ChimeraX. We explicitly require saving the corrected TeX file and successful compilation.

12. TeXstudio C-02: Single-letter correction.

The task asks the agent to correct a typo in the deduction rules of the λ​C\lambda C type system by changing exactly one letter. We retain this restriction and add saving and successful compilation to the instruction.

13. TeXstudio C-03: Figure-path repair.

The task asks the agent to repair the incomplete figure path figs/lat. We add the requirements to save the TeX file and verify successful compilation.

14. TeXstudio C-04: Figure width and completion requirements.

The original English instruction misspells “width” as “with.” We correct the typo, retain the restriction to change only the width of figs/envelope to 0.48, and explicitly require saving and successful compilation.

15. TeXstudio C-05: Lean code correction.

The task asks the agent to correct Lean 4 code in the article by changing exactly one word, with the supplied VS Code available for debugging. We correct “exact one word” to “exactly one word” and add the requirements to save the TeX file and ensure successful compilation.

G.2 Task & Answer Errors

These repairs correct task statements, reference answers, labeled test points, and expected results encoded in evaluators, including mathematical statements with insufficient assumptions.

16. KAlgebra C-07: Evaluating the wrong derivative.

The task asks for the derivative of f⁡(x)=ln⁡(x+1)+x2−xf(x)=\ln(x+1)+x^{2}-x, but the original evaluator uses labels corresponding to the derivative of ln⁡(x2+1)+x2−x\ln(x^{2}+1)+x^{2}-x. We rebuild the test points using

f′​(x)=1x+1+2​x−1,f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{1}{x+1}+2x-1,

with positive examples inside the original function’s domain.

17. KAlgebra C-12: Incorrect positive points for a distance-product curve.

The product of the Euclidean distances to (1,0)(1,0) and (−1,0)(-1,0) must equal 16, giving the implicit equation

((x−1)2+y2)​((x+1)2+y2)=256.\bigl((x-1)^{2}+y^{2}\bigr)\bigl((x+1)^{2}+y^{2}\bigr)=256.

The original positive examples do not lie on this curve. We recompute their coordinates according to the stated condition.

18. KAlgebra C-14: Confusing diameter with radius.

The stated diameter is 2​22\sqrt{2}, so the radius is 2\sqrt{2} and the sphere satisfies x2+y2+z2=2x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=2. The original labels instead correspond to x2+y2+z2=8x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=8, treating the diameter as the radius. We replace the test points to distinguish the requested sphere from the incorrect one.

19. Celestia C-09: Apparent-magnitude answer inconsistent with the software.

The original reference answer is 4.47. In the benchmark’s initial environment, sorting the galaxy list by distance and excluding the Milky Way selects Sagittarius dSph, whose displayed apparent magnitude is 3.84. We update the answer to 3.84 and specify that the answer must come from Celestia’s Celestial Browser, excluding the Milky Way itself.

20. Celestia D-02: Eclipse date and answer format.

The original answer gives December 21 for the last lunar eclipse of 2056; we correct it to December 22. The revised instruction also specifies the UTC date at maximum eclipse as seen from Earth and requests only the numeric day of December, removing ambiguity about the event time and submission format.

21. ChimeraX C-04: Incorrect hydrogen count.

The task asks for the number of hydrogen atoms in /A:1. We correct the reference answer from 12 to 0 and update the evaluator accordingly.

22. Lean 4 A-02: Overly strong Ackermann inequality.

The original statement requires ack⁡(x,y+1)<ack⁡(x+1,y)\operatorname{ack}(x,y+1)<\operatorname{ack}(x+1,y). Equality can occur when y=0y=0, so the strict inequality is false. We replace << with ≤\leq.

23. Lean 4 C-05: Incorrect set-containment assumptions.

The original assumptions A⊆YA\subseteq Y and Y⊆A𝖼Y\subseteq A^{\mathsf{c}} do not imply that YY is compact. For example, when A=∅A=\emptyset, they permit noncompact closed sets YY. We replace these containment conditions with Y⊆AY\subseteq A, retaining compactness of AA and closedness of YY, so that the statement expresses compactness of a closed subset of a compact set.

24. Lean 4 D-02: Missing convexity assumption.

The original statement tries to derive uniform continuity on SS from a bounded derivative on SS, without conditions connecting its points. We add Convex ℝ​S\mathbb{R}\;S, allowing the derivative bound to control function differences through a mean-value inequality and support the uniform-continuity conclusion.

25. Lean 4 D-07: Moment condition does not express integrability.

The original statement binds XX twice and uses an equality between an expectation and some real number MM without explicitly requiring the necessary integrability. We remove the duplicate binding and assume that ω↦|X⁡(ω)|p\omega\mapsto|X(\omega)|^{p} is integrable with respect to ℙ\mathbb{P}, supporting the tail conclusion

xp​ℙ​(|X|>x)⟶0(x→+∞).x^{p}\,\mathbb{P}\bigl(|X|>x\bigr)\longrightarrow 0\qquad(x\to+\infty).
26. Lean 4 E-03: Hamiltonian endpoints and edge bound.

The original hypothesis requires a Hamiltonian walk between every pair of vertices, including identical endpoints. We restrict it to distinct vertices. The extra constant term +1+1 in the original conclusion is also invalid: K4K_{4} satisfies the revised hypothesis but has 2​e=3​n2e=3n. We therefore correct the conclusion to 2​e≥3​n2e\geq 3n for n≥4n\geq 4.

27. GRASS GIS D-01: Incorrect expected schema type.

The task requests a COLOR varchar column, which the current GRASS GIS and SQLite environment reports as TEXT through v.db.select. The original evaluator instead expects CHARACTER. We retain the requested varchar declaration and change the expected schema type to TEXT. The evaluator already supports both GUI and Console execution; this repair corrects the expected result.

G.3 Evaluator Bias

These repairs remove unnecessary evaluator restrictions on execution paths, output representations, and output locations while preserving the task requirements. For GRASS GIS B-03–B-10, we verified that both GUI operations and Console commands achieve the required outcomes. However, the original evaluators rely on GUI property caches and reject equivalent Console executions when those caches are not populated. We extend the checks to recognize both paths. TeXstudio B-04 addresses overly strict matching of BibTeX title capitalization and formatting. GRASS GIS B-12 extends output checking to a separate statistics window. Tasks that explicitly require a GUI state change retain checks of that state.

28. GRASS GIS B-03: Category and topology display.

The original evaluator reads display from the layer-properties cache. An equivalent d.vect command can produce the requested display without populating that cache. We inspect either GUI parameters or layer command state for both cat and topo, excluding states marked hidden or unchecked.

29. GRASS GIS B-04: Area fill color.

The task requires the fill color (191,191,191)(191,191,191). In addition to GUI parameters, we inspect fill_color or fcolor in the layer’s d.vect command. The evaluator accepts RGB notation and the equivalent RGBA notation with an opaque alpha value.

30. GRASS GIS B-05: Road line color.

The task requires white lines for roadsmajor. We inspect GUI parameters or layer command state and accept white, 255:255:255, and the equivalent opaque RGBA representation.

31. GRASS GIS B-06: Railway line width.

A Console command can set the railroads line width to 2 while leaving the GUI parameter cache empty. We add checks of layer command state and accept both 2 and 2.0.

32. GRASS GIS B-07: Fire-station symbol.

The task requires the basic/marker symbol for firestations. We check the icon parameter in either GUI properties or the layer’s d.vect command, allowing an equivalent Console result to be recognized.

33. GRASS GIS B-08: Hospital symbol size.

The task requires symbol size 10 for hospitals. We additionally inspect the command’s size parameter and accept both 10 and 10.0, removing dependence on editing the GUI property panel.

34. GRASS GIS B-09: School filtering condition.

The task requires displaying schools satisfying the wheelchair-access condition. We inspect where in either GUI parameters or layer command state and remove whitespace before comparison with wheelchair=’yes’.

35. GRASS GIS B-10: Label configuration.

The task requires the boundary_region label field NOME, font Ubuntu:Bold, and horizontal alignment center. Console execution can produce the requested display while leaving the GUI cache empty. We check all three settings in either GUI parameters or the same layer command, recognizing both completion paths.

36. GRASS GIS B-12: Statistics in a separate output window.

The original evaluator searches only dump[’output’] for n: 263975. We retain that check and add a fallback for a separate r.univar window. The fallback uses the accessibility tree to identify the target map and selected Command output tab, then checks the corresponding image region for rendered output, covering cases where the output is absent from the original field.

37. TeXstudio B-04: Overly strict BibTeX title matching.

The task asks the agent to obtain a paper’s BibTeX from Google Scholar and write it to refs.bib. The original evaluator requires exact title capitalization and spacing around the equals sign, rejecting valid entries for the same paper with equivalent textual representations. We make title matching case-insensitive and allow whitespace around the equals sign. The instruction also explicitly requires saving refs.bib.

G.4 Environment Repairs

This category covers repairs to the evaluation environment, including application-usage prompts, answer-submission protocols, action-response handling, compilation, and initialization settings. It also records the removal of one task requiring an unavailable external account. These shared repairs are not counted as additional task revisions.

38. ChimeraX D-03: External account required for AlphaFold.

The task asks for an AlphaFold structure prediction from a supplied amino-acid sequence. Completion requires an external Google account that is not provided by the benchmark environment. We remove this task from the final evaluation set.

Answer-submission protocol (32 tasks).

We observed correct answers being rejected because their response format was not correctly handled by the framework. The original prompt did not sufficiently specify the code-block structure required for ANS submissions. This protocol issue affects all 32 answer-submission tasks. We explicitly require ANS followed by the actual answer inside a separate fenced code block, with neither the answer on the fence line nor additional text outside the block.

Application-usage prompts.

The original LEAN_VM_USAGE incorrectly contains TeXstudio document-editing instructions, while TEXSTUDIO_VM_USAGE is undefined. We provide the correct Lean 4 instructions: complete the target proof or code in VS Code, save the file, and use Lean feedback to check for errors, warnings caused by sorry, and remaining goals. We also restore the TeXstudio-specific document-editing and compilation instructions.

Malformed action responses.

The original framework does not validate unsupported tool or scratchpad control markers, so responses containing duplicated actions inside such envelopes can be parsed as ordinary action text. We reject these responses before emitting any actions and allow one retry with the same observation. The recovery prompt asks the agent to follow the existing action format without unsupported envelopes or duplicated draft and final content.

TeXstudio compilation environment.

We repair the TeXstudio compilation environment so that compilation checks can run normally, preventing an environment failure from blocking task completion and evaluation.

GRASS GIS initial pointer position.

At initialization, the mouse pointer originally obscured the Console area, interfering with observation and evaluation. We reposition it near the center of the interface so that the Console remains unobstructed.

Update notifications.

An update dialog appeared after every initialization. Dismissing it consumed interaction steps and materially interfered with evaluation by using part of the task’s step budget on an unrelated action. We disable updates to prevent these recurring dialogs and their associated evaluation overhead.

Appendix H Task Construction and Deduplication

We construct 108 additional tasks across the six scientific applications for skill self-evolution. These tasks use the same types of software operations as the test tasks to support the transfer of operational experience, while varying the target objects, task parameters, or specific requirements to form distinct tasks. We manually compare each additional task against the ScienceBoard-Verified tasks, examining its goal, initial state, required output, and evaluation criteria to confirm that it does not duplicate a test task. Researchers in the corresponding scientific domains who are familiar with the respective software manually review and execute all additional tasks to verify that their requirements are clear, their reference answers or target states are correct, and they can be completed in the specified software environments.

Appendix I Execution-Guided Skill Self-Evolution: Additional Details

This appendix specifies the execution protocol used in Section 3.2. Evolution uses only E=Expanded∖VerifiedE=\mathrm{Expanded}\setminus\mathrm{Verified} and the original resources 𝒟\mathcal{D}. For new-knowledge creation, 𝒟\mathcal{D} is accessed through bounded live browsing that starts from the configured official documentation root for the current application and follows only in-scope links discovered from fetched official pages. It does not use a search engine, BM25 retrieval, a saved Resource-to-Skill snapshot, or model knowledge as source evidence. The execution model is fixed, and V=VerifiedV=\mathrm{Verified} is reserved for final evaluation.

I.1 Frozen Initial Library and Per-Task State

All evolution tasks start from the same frozen initial library ℒ0=(𝒮0,ℛ0)\mathcal{L}_{0}=(\mathcal{S}_{0},\mathcal{R}_{0}). A task never installs a provisional update into the library used by another task. Instead, it maintains a private execution history and may contribute at most one independently validated candidate to a global candidate pool 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Candidates are consolidated only after all tasks terminate.

For each task qq, its first task exploration selects a fixed routed set ℱq\mathcal{F}_{q} of Skills and References from ℒ0\mathcal{L}_{0}. Later task explorations use the same routed names and initial versions, even after the task has produced a failed candidate. This separates behavioral exploration from candidate installation: rejected knowledge remains evidence, not active guidance.

Each candidate contains one complete target entry relative to ℒ0\mathcal{L}_{0}. A candidate produced after a failed exploration may revise one entry in ℱq\mathcal{F}_{q} or add one Skill or Reference supported by 𝒟\mathcal{D}. A candidate distilled after a later successful exploration may only revise one existing routed entry. A rejected candidate is never used as the textual base of a later candidate.

I.2 Complete Execution History and Input Separation

Each task has an indexed history archive. For every task exploration and candidate validation, the archive records the task instruction, execution type, exact execution-time prompt, raw action–observation trajectory, evaluator outcome, routed Skill and Reference names, their complete execution-time contents and version hashes, and every screenshot mapped to its trajectory step. When applicable, it also records the diagnosis and the complete candidate entry used in validation. Screenshots are interpreted as pre-action observations: the effect of an action is checked in the following screenshot.

The first task exploration receives no history. Every later task exploration receives all earlier task explorations and candidate validations for that task, including their exact prompts, raw trajectories, diagnoses, candidates, outcomes, and screenshots. The records are explicitly labeled so that the agent can distinguish exploration from validation, identify which knowledge version was loaded, and map each screenshot to its execution and step. All historical screenshots are placed in the first model turn and marked as evidence; the final live screenshot remains the state on which the agent must act. The prompt instructs the agent to inspect the complete history, avoid repeating failed action sequences, and not follow initial Skills or References mechanically when current GUI evidence suggests a version mismatch.

Diagnosis and knowledge writing receive the task, loaded entries, exact prompt, raw trajectory, evaluator result, and complete screenshot sequence. The analysis agent must inspect every screenshot before submitting its result. Candidate validation is deliberately separated: it receives no exploration history, successful trajectory, diagnosis, or candidate rationale. This prevents the validation agent from succeeding through transient trajectory memory rather than through the proposed external knowledge.

I.3 Task Exploration, Failure Diagnosis, and Candidate Validation

Let i∈{1,…,Mexplore}i\in\{1,\ldots,M_{\mathrm{explore}}\} index task explorations for task qq. Each exploration begins from the standard initial environment in a fresh session:

τq(i)=Executeθ⁡(q,ℒ0,ℱq,ℋq(i)),\tau_{q}^{(i)}=\operatorname{Execute}_{\theta}\bigl(q;\mathcal{L}_{0},\mathcal{F}_{q},\mathcal{H}_{q}^{(i)}\bigr), (3)

where ℋq(1)=∅\mathcal{H}_{q}^{(1)}=\emptyset and ℋq(i)\mathcal{H}_{q}^{(i)} for i>1i>1 contains all earlier exploration and candidate-validation records for qq. Routing is performed normally only for i=1i=1; its result defines ℱq\mathcal{F}_{q} for subsequent exploration and validation.

If τq(1)\tau_{q}^{(1)} succeeds, the task exits without proposing an update. A successful exploration with i>1i>1 enters the submission process in Appendix I.4. Each failed exploration is analyzed for one primary root cause. Exhausting the action budget, stopping early, or failing the evaluator describes the observed outcome rather than the underlying cause. The diagnosis uses exactly three categories:

  1. 1.

    Grounding failure (grounding_failure). Incorrect interface localization, targeting, state reading, or manipulation is the principal obstacle. Repeated grounding mistakes that consume the action budget can qualify. The counterfactual criterion is whether correcting those grounding mistakes would remove the principal obstacle; if an independent knowledge deficiency would remain, a knowledge category must be selected instead.

  2. 2.

    Modify existing knowledge (modify_existing). One loaded Skill or Reference is relevant but contains an erroneous or incomplete procedure, omitted condition, inappropriate parameter, unsupported syntax, or version-dependent instruction. The target must be one entry in ℱq\mathcal{F}_{q}.

  3. 3.

    Add new knowledge (add_new_knowledge). The routed entries do not contain the capability or operational knowledge needed for the task. This category is reserved for a genuine coverage gap rather than a minor defect in a relevant entry. The new Skill or Reference must be supported by task-relevant content in the original resources 𝒟\mathcal{D}; without sufficient source support, no candidate is produced.

Diagnosis and conditional candidate writing occur in the same analysis session. The diagnosis step fixes the category, evidence, and proposed repair. For modify_existing, it also fixes the type and name of one routed target, after which the next step writes its complete replacement while retaining access to the same trajectory and screenshots. For add_new_knowledge, the diagnosis deliberately leaves the target type and name unspecified and describes only the missing reusable knowledge scope. Only after this diagnosis is accepted does the same session unlock bounded live access to 𝒟\mathcal{D}; the research step determines whether the supported artifact is a Skill or Reference, chooses its stable title, and writes one complete new entry. If the fetched official material is insufficient, no candidate is produced. A grounding diagnosis likewise produces no candidate and therefore requires no candidate validation. Either no-candidate outcome consumes the current exploration attempt. If another exploration remains, the task continues with its accumulated history. Even after the final allowed exploration fails, its diagnosis and, when applicable, its one candidate validation are still completed.

Independent Candidate Validation

For a candidate Δq(i)\Delta_{q}^{(i)}, validation constructs a temporary library

ℒ~q(i)=ℒ0⊕Δq(i),\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{q}^{(i)}=\mathcal{L}_{0}\oplus\Delta_{q}^{(i)}, (4)

where ⊕\oplus replaces the target’s initial version for a revision or inserts one source-supported entry for an addition. The validation agent starts from the task’s standard initial environment in a fresh session. It force-loads the original entries named by ℱq\mathcal{F}_{q}; for a revision, the candidate replaces its corresponding original entry, and for an addition, the candidate is force-loaded in addition to all original routed entries. Thus every attempt contains at most one modified or new target.

The validation trajectory is

τ~q(i)=Executeθ⁡(q,ℒ~q(i),ℱ~q(i),∅),\widetilde{\tau}_{q}^{(i)}=\operatorname{Execute}_{\theta}\bigl(q;\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{q}^{(i)},\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}_{q}^{(i)},\emptyset\bigr), (5)

where the empty history excludes all prior trajectories, screenshots, diagnoses, and rationales. The task evaluator alone determines success. A successful candidate is added to 𝒫\mathcal{P} and the task terminates. A failed candidate, its complete contents, and its validation record are archived; if another task exploration remains, that exploration again uses ℒ0\mathcal{L}_{0} and ℱq\mathcal{F}_{q}, with the failed validation supplied only as history.

I.4 Submission After History-Guided Success

A task exploration that succeeds at i>1i>1 may have relied on failure history unavailable at deployment. The submission agent therefore contrasts the successful exploration with all earlier failed explorations, candidate validations, loaded knowledge versions, and candidate contents. In one response it either concludes that no knowledge change is warranted or writes a complete revision to one existing entry in ℱq\mathcal{F}_{q}. This process cannot create a new Skill or Reference.

At most MsubmitM_{\mathrm{submit}} submission attempts are allowed. Every revised candidate is generated from the target’s version in ℒ0\mathcal{L}_{0}, not by editing the preceding rejected submission candidate. On later attempts, the submission agent additionally receives all previous submission candidates and their validation trajectories so that it can avoid repeating an ineffective revision. Each candidate is validated through the history-free protocol in Equation 5. The first successful candidate enters 𝒫\mathcal{P} and ends the task.

When the submission agent attributes a failed validation to grounding, it may retain the same candidate and validate it again; the unchanged retry consumes one submission attempt. If no candidate has yet been proposed, it may instead validate the unchanged initial routed knowledge. Success of this unchanged validation ends the task without adding a candidate. If all MsubmitM_{\mathrm{submit}} attempts fail, the task terminates without an update and does not return to task exploration.

I.5 Candidate Consolidation and Final Evaluation

After every evolution task terminates, accepted candidates are grouped by target Skill or Reference. Revisions are grouped by the identity of their original entry. For additions, a conservative Grok semantic-deduplication pass groups candidates only when they have the same knowledge type and express the same reusable capability at substantially the same granularity, scope, and intended use; Skills and References are never grouped together, and uncertain candidates remain separate. Each group adopts the title of one independently validated member rather than inventing a new title. If this auxiliary grouping call is technically unavailable or violates its structured-output contract, the pipeline fails open to exact type-and-title grouping, thereby avoiding an unsupported merge. Different targets are consolidated independently and are never mixed merely because they came from the same task.

If a target has exactly one accepted candidate, that already validated candidate is adopted directly without another task execution. If a target has multiple candidates, the consolidation model receives every accepted candidate and either the target’s complete initial content for a revision or an explicit new-entry baseline for an addition. It then produces one complete entry that preserves the independently validated, non-conflicting improvements of all candidates. The merged text is not allowed to discard a candidate-specific capability merely to simplify the entry.

Because merging can change individually validated content, a multi-candidate consolidation must pass regression certification. Let QgQ_{g} contain all tasks that contributed candidates to consolidated target gg. The same consolidated content and hash are installed for every replay, and each q∈Qgq\in Q_{g} is executed from its standard initial environment in a fresh, history-free session with its first-exploration routing fixed. The initial full replay over QgQ_{g} does not consume the reflection budget.

If every replay succeeds, the target is certified. Otherwise, a reflection agent receives the initial entry, all accepted candidates, the current consolidation, and every regression prompt, raw trajectory, evaluator outcome, and screenshot. It chooses between two actions:

  1. 1.

    Revise. If the consolidated content caused or contributed to any failure, a complete replacement is regenerated from the initial entry and all accepted candidates rather than edited cumulatively from the failed consolidation. Previously passed results are invalidated, and all tasks in QgQ_{g} are replayed.

  2. 2.

    Keep. The current consolidation may be retained only when every current failure is attributable to grounding and the content itself requires no change. Passed tasks remain certified, and only the failed tasks are replayed.

Each reflection followed by its required replay consumes one of at most MconsolidationM_{\mathrm{consolidation}} cycles. Infrastructure or API failures are handled separately and are not treated as task failures. If certification still fails after the allowance is exhausted, target gg is rejected: a revised target retains its initial version, while an uncertified addition is omitted. After all target groups are resolved, ℒfinal=Consolidate⁡(ℒ0,𝒫)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{final}}=\operatorname{Consolidate}(\mathcal{L}_{0},\mathcal{P}) is frozen and evaluated on VV with standard initial environments, fresh sessions, normal routing, and no evolution history. No additional global regression is performed.

I.6 Stopping Conditions and Budgets

The default configuration uses

Mexplore=3,Msubmit=3,Mconsolidation=3.M_{\mathrm{explore}}=3,\qquad M_{\mathrm{submit}}=3,\qquad M_{\mathrm{consolidation}}=3. (6)

Only task explorations consume MexploreM_{\mathrm{explore}}; their diagnosis, candidate writing, and one independent candidate validation do not. Only submission validations consume MsubmitM_{\mathrm{submit}}. The initial regression of a multi-candidate consolidation does not consume MconsolidationM_{\mathrm{consolidation}}; each subsequent reflection-and-replay cycle does.

Excluding consolidation replay, a conservative execution bound is

Nexec≤|E|(2​Mexplore+Msubmit),N_{\mathrm{exec}}\leq|E|\bigl(2M_{\mathrm{explore}}+M_{\mathrm{submit}}\bigr), (7)

which counts at most one candidate validation after each task exploration and at most MsubmitM_{\mathrm{submit}} submission validations. This is intentionally loose because a task that enters submission cannot also fail all task explorations. For a multi-candidate consolidation group gg, regression adds at most (1+Mconsolidation)​|Qg|(1+M_{\mathrm{consolidation}})|Q_{g}| task executions; keep decisions can reduce this by retaining already passed tasks. These bounds exclude final evaluation, diagnosis and writing calls, source retrieval, routing, and separately limited infrastructure retries.

Evolution outcomes and consolidation replays are process measurements and are not substituted for held-out evaluation results.

Appendix K Case Study: How Self-Evolve Repairs Resource–Environment Mismatches and Improves Task Performance

We use KAlgebra surface-plotting tasks to examine how a mismatch between available documentation and the deployed software affects the initial Skills and References, and how Self-Evolve addresses it through execution feedback. Tasks B-14 and C-19 in Expanded–Verified expose the initial failures and support Skill revision. We then examine whether the frozen updated Skill helps previously failed tasks in the disjoint Verified set succeed. All runs use Grok 4.6 (xhigh).

K.1 Resource–Environment Mismatch: Why Self-Evolve Is Needed

Resource-to-Skill organizes documented procedures into callable Skills and References, but their applicability depends on whether the documentation describes the deployed environment. During resource collection, we could not retrieve documentation matching the deployed software version and used the relevant documentation available to us. The resulting resources therefore describe a different software version.

The collected KAlgebra handbook states: “Z cannot be defined yet. For the moment KAlgebra only supports 3D graphs explicitly dependent only on the x and y.” The initial Skill, Plot an explicit x-and-y 3D surface, incorporates this restriction as a precondition, while the associated 3D Graph Reference retains the documented guidance. As the later executions demonstrate, the deployed software also accepts three-variable mappings and implicit equations involving zz.

Source documentation. The collected handbook restricts 3D plotting to explicit dependence on xx and yy. This restriction is inherited by the initial resources but does not describe the deployed environment’s full input capabilities.

B-14: initial execution under the routed resources.

The task is to plot 2​x2+3​y2−z2=12x^{2}+3y^{2}-z^{2}=1. The model initially routes to the 3D-plotting Skill and two References: the function catalog and the 3D Graph reference. Following the explicit-only guidance, the first exploration enters (x,y)->root(2*xˆ2+3*yˆ2-1,2). This selects only the positive root and plots one branch; the task fails. This initial exploration uses no failure history or revised Skill.

B-14, initial state. The 3D Graph input is empty.

After entering the root mapping. Only one branch is plotted; evaluation fails.

C-19: initial execution under the routed resources.

The task is to plot a sphere with diameter endpoints A⁡(1,−2,3)A(1,-2,3) and B⁡(5,2,−1)B(5,2,-1). Its center is (3,0,1)(3,0,1) and its squared radius is 1212. The initial Skill and routed 3D Graph Reference likewise direct the first exploration toward an explicit mapping. The positive-root expression produces only the upper hemisphere. Zooming out does not change the incomplete surface, and the task fails. This exploration also precedes any failure-history input or Skill revision.

C-19, initial state. The 3D Graph is empty.

After entering the positive-root mapping. Only the upper hemisphere is plotted.

After zooming out. The sphere remains incomplete.

End-of-exploration checkpoint. The incomplete sphere remains; evaluation fails.

Implication for the initial resources.

Both trajectories show how the documented restriction narrows the agent’s solution path to explicit z=f⁡(x,y)z=f(x,y) expressions. For these tasks, a single root branch covers only part of the required surface. An accepted expression and a visible plot therefore do not establish task completion. These failures motivate using actual execution to test and revise the inherited procedural constraints.

K.2 From Execution Failure to Skill Revision

B-14 and C-19 belong to the Expanded–Verified evolution set. Throughout exploration, the initial library and each task’s first routed resource set remain fixed. After failure, the system retains the execution trajectory, screenshots, evaluator result, diagnosis, and candidate-validation records. Later explorations receive the accumulated history for that task, with historical executions explicitly identified and their mapped screenshots included in the prompt. They can therefore reconsider unsuccessful actions while still starting from the original routed resources.

Candidate revisions are tested separately in fresh environments without exploration history. After a successful exploration, the submission step uses that trajectory and the earlier failures to revise the original Skill, followed by another independent validation. The discovered procedure must thus be written into the Skill and reproduce success without access to prior trajectories or diagnoses. The following sections continue from the initial failures shown above.

Self-Evolve uses the failure history to discover procedures supported by the deployed environment and incorporates them into independently validated Skills. Appendix L Case Study: Adding a Module-Level Reference for GRASS GIS

Why broad resource coverage leaves a task-relevant gap.

The GRASS GIS Reference Manual organizes software knowledge into twelve major sections. The benchmark tasks, however, are concentrated in a much smaller part of this space, primarily the Graphical User Interface (including Display), General, 3D raster processing, and Database sections. Resource-to-Skill runs before the downstream task distribution is known, so its initial construction aims to cover the software broadly. This coverage-oriented strategy can produce Skills and References for material that benchmark tasks rarely use, while leaving frequently needed leaf-level knowledge too general to execute. The d.vect command illustrates this mismatch: the initial Display catalog identifies the command but does not provide the syntax and parameter combinations needed by the recurring vector-styling tasks.

The manual spans twelve major sections; task demand is concentrated in a subset. The d.vect command is documented under Display.

Prior Verified runs expose a recurring gap in this task family. B-04 requires an area fill color, B-06 a line width, and B-08 a point-symbol size. Their initial routed resources contained a broad Display command catalog, but the corresponding executions did not reach the required d.vect parameters. These failures motivate adding knowledge at the module level rather than writing a separate task-specific procedure for each map.

B-18: diagnosing and filling the knowledge gap.

B-18 is an Expanded–Verified task in the evolution set: “Display countries@PERMANENT as red boundary lines only in GRASS GIS.” The initial resource set exposed the broad Display catalog, but not enough executable detail to compose the required command. Grok Build examined the failure evidence and the official GRASS manual, then selected a Reference rather than a Skill. The diagnosis was that the missing capability was declarative module knowledge—command syntax, option semantics, accepted values, defaults, and parameter composition—rather than an unlearned multi-step workflow. Grok Build browsed three pages from the same official manual. All 12 retained source-evidence records passed the later source audit, and the generator did not receive Verified task prompts or answers.

The resulting module-level Reference, d.vect Vector Display and Styling, generalizes beyond the B-18 map and color. Its relevant guidance includes:

color=name controls feature color; fill_color=name controls area fill. Areas use fill_color for their fill and color for their outline. Use fill_color=none to make areas transparent, or color=none to suppress area outlines.
width=integer sets line width (default: 0).
size=float sets point-symbol size (default: 5).
attribute_column=name selects the label column; font, xref, and related options control label appearance and placement.

This knowledge is directly relevant to several task families: independent outline and fill controls support B-18 and B-04; line-width and symbol-size options support B-06 and B-08; label parameters provide a reusable route for other vector-styling requests. The Reference describes reusable d.vect behavior rather than a fixed answer to B-18 in the evolution set: its options can be composed for other maps, colors, and styling requests.

B-18 validation: applying the added module knowledge.

During validation, the candidate Reference is force-injected into B-18’s resource set. Using the command syntax and independent outline and fill controls provided by the Reference, the agent constructs the command below and executes it in the Command Console. The map is rendered with red boundaries and no area fill, and B-18 passes. The added Reference supplies the parameter knowledge missing from the initial catalog, enabling the agent to compose the required command.

d.vect map=countries@PERMANENT type=boundary color=red fill_color=none

B-18: using the added Reference, the agent renders red boundaries with no area fill.

Transfer to Verified: three related styling tasks.

B-04, B-06, and B-08 all failed in earlier Verified runs with the initial library. After validation, the new d.vect Reference was made available in the evolved library. In the subsequent Verified evaluation, resource selection was free: each task routed to the new Reference. The successful runs used three different parameter families:

Task Initial gap Command in a successful transfer run
B-04 Could not set area fill color d.vect map=boundary_region fill_color=191:191:191
B-06 Did not set width=2 d.vect map=railroads width=2
B-08 Did not set size=10 d.vect map=hospitals size=10

B-04: the area is gray after applying fill_color=191:191:191.

B-06: the Console executes width=2.

B-08: the Console executes size=10.

Takeaway.

This case shows how Self-Evolve addresses the mismatch between the broad scope of source resources and the specific knowledge required by downstream tasks through knowledge addition. The initial library covered GRASS GIS broadly but omitted the d.vect details required by these tasks. Execution feedback from the evolution set guided Grok Build to add a reusable module-level Reference. The added knowledge filled this task-relevant gap, enabling success on B-18 and related Verified tasks that the initial library had failed to support.

Appendix M Case Study: Outdated Interface Guidance in Celestia

Task A-05 asks the agent to display dwarf-planet orbits but not moon orbits in Celestia. We examine an initial-library run by Grok-4.6 (xhigh), before any Skill or Reference evolution. The first-stage router selected the Skill Control rendering features and display quality with keyboard shortcuts and the Reference Celestia label, info-text, constellation, and star-filter controls. The source User’s Guide describes Celestia 1.6.1, whereas the target environment runs Celestia 1.7.0 with a Qt interface.

From source guidance to the target interface.

The selected Reference places the checkboxes for orbit categories in the lower part of a View Options window and also mentions the O key for orbit paths. The selected Skill condenses this guidance to pressing O to toggle planet orbits; it does not explain how to choose dwarf-planet or moon orbits separately in the target interface. Figure 6 shows the old View Options window in the source guide. In the deployed Qt interface, neither the Display nor the View menu contains this window. Instead, the toolbar’s O dropdown exposes separate checkboxes for Dwarf Planets and Moons (Figure 7). The target-interface screenshot is an independent illustration of the available control, not a frame from the failed run.

Execution with the initial Skill and Reference.

Figure 8 presents every screenshot from the five-action run. Each screenshot is a pre-action observation; its caption describes the action chosen next. Although the toolbar’s O control is visible in the initial state, the agent first states that Display should contain View Options and opens that menu. Finding no such entry, it moves to View, retries View with Alt+V, and then selects Guides as another possible location for orbit-path options. That action hides the toolbar. Only in its final response does the agent identify the O dropdown, but it attempts to restore the toolbar rather than configure the two orbit categories. The run ends without completing A-05, and the task evaluator reports failure.

(a) Initial state. The toolbar’s O control is visible; the agent chooses to open Display.

(b) Display menu. No View Options appears; the agent turns to View.

(c) After clicking View. The menu is not open; the agent retries with Alt+V.

(d) View menu. The old entry is absent here too; the agent selects Guides.

(e) After selecting Guides. The toolbar has disappeared; the agent next tries to restore it.

Implication.

This run makes the cost of outdated knowledge concrete. Guidance inherited from the old interface directs the agent toward Display, View, and Guides, consuming its limited action budget even though the target’s O dropdown is visible from the start. The agent recognizes that control only at the end and does not complete the category-specific orbit settings. Thus, an initial Skill and Reference grounded in documentation can still waste execution steps and lead to task failure when their operational guidance does not match the deployed software.

Appendix N Task Requirements and Documentation Scope for Lean 4 and TeXstudio

This appendix compares the Verified task requirements for Lean 4 and TeXstudio with the documentation used to construct their initial Skills and References. Tables 10 and 11 summarize the task goals; the full task instructions are provided with ScienceBoard-VE. The comparison helps explain why additional knowledge from the same software-specific sources provides more limited gains for these applications in Table 3.

N.1 Lean 4: General Proof Guidance and Domain-Specific Theorems

The Lean 4 initial library is constructed from Theorem Proving in Lean 4 (https://leanprover.github.io/theorem_proving_in_lean4/). As Figure 9 shows, its contents cover general proof methods, including propositions, quantifiers, tactics, induction, and type classes. The Verified tasks in Table 10, by contrast, ask the agent to complete particular formal statements across set theory, algebra, topology, analysis, measure theory, and other mathematical domains. Completing them requires identifying applicable domain definitions and lemmas and assembling proofs that match the given Lean declarations.

The source supplies general Lean proof and interaction knowledge, but it cannot directly enumerate the domain-specific lemmas and proof sequences required by all of these statements. Execution feedback can expose where an attempted proof fails; when the original source does not contain the missing mathematical knowledge, source-grounded additions to the library have limited scope. This task–source gap helps explain why Lean 4 retains a relatively low success rate after self-evolution.

N.2 TeXstudio: Editor Operations and Cross-Application Information

The TeXstudio initial library is constructed from the TeXstudio manual (https://texstudio-org.github.io/). Its contents cover document editing, compilation, PDF viewing, and editor configuration (Figure 10). Table 11 shows that some Verified tasks require only TeX editing or compilation, while others first require a measurement, object property, computation, or bibliographic record from another application or website.

Many tasks therefore have two components: obtaining the content to insert and editing or compiling the TeX document. TeXstudio documentation can support the latter, but it does not supply measurements or object information from other scientific applications. A library constructed and evolved from TeXstudio documentation alone cannot cover all of these cross-application requirements, which helps explain its more limited improvement in Table 3.

Appendix O Research Setting and Baseline Reproduction Constraints of Resource2Skill

O.1 Research Setting and Knowledge Objectives

Resource2Skill and ScienceCUA both investigate how to transform human-created resources into reusable skills, but they differ in their research settings and knowledge objectives.

Resource2Skill primarily addresses authoring tasks across domains such as PPT, Web, Excel, Blender, CAD, UE5, and audio production. It distills skills from tutorial videos, repositories, articles, documentation, and reference artifacts. Its library provides retrievable and composable authoring techniques, code patterns, and visual references to help agents create new artifacts, with downstream evaluation primarily measuring artifact quality.

ScienceCUA aims to improve the ability of models and agents to operate scientific software. Starting from supplied PDF/HTML software documentation, it discovers supported operational tasks, derives task-level procedures, and organizes shared knowledge such as commands, syntax, and parameter constraints. These forms of knowledge are represented as Skills and References, respectively, to support agents in completing user tasks in deployed software environments. Downstream evaluation primarily measures task success.

Thus, although both approaches investigate resource-to-skill construction, they differ in how resources are used, how knowledge is organized, and what downstream evaluation emphasizes.

O.2 Limitations in Adapting the Released Implementation

At the implementation level, the relevant public interfaces of Resource2Skill do not directly provide the document-level knowledge-construction process required for our collections of PDF/HTML software documentation. Although the paper describes a construction operator that can generate multiple candidate skills from a single resource, the two interfaces directly relevant to our documentation inputs have the following limitations in the public code we inspected.

  1. 1.

    StaticArtifactConnector does not directly support PDF manual parsing. Its directory mode filters files using domain-specific extension lists, covering .xlsx, .html/.htm, .pptx, .blend, and selected audio and project formats, but excluding PDF. Consequently, the KAlgebra and Celestia PDF manuals used in our experiments cannot be directly processed through this mode. Its catalogue mode constructs candidates from supplied JSON fields, including descriptions and applicability; it does not itself parse the referenced manuals, discover knowledge units, or generate operational knowledge. StaticArtifactConnector implementation.

  2. 2.

    ArticleConnector uses individual supplied pages as candidate-generation units. It accepts a URL list, fetches each page, and produces at most one CandidateSkill per URL. Its optional model call primarily extracts a title, applicability, tags, and a short summary. The interface does not implement recursive documentation crawling, cross-page evidence aggregation, or the discovery of multiple procedural knowledge units within a page. Supplying a documentation homepage or a list of page URLs therefore does not directly provide a complete workflow for constructing operational knowledge from an entire documentation collection. ArticleConnector implementation.

Adapting these interfaces to our setting would require additional components for PDF parsing, HTML documentation discovery and collection, knowledge-unit decomposition, cross-page content organization, and procedural-content generation, before packaging the results as CandidateSkill records. Resource2Skill’s subsequent candidate processing and Skill Wiki construction remain reusable. However, the added components would directly determine the content, granularity, and coverage of the resulting library—properties central to the evaluation of resource-to-skill construction.

Such an adaptation would therefore extend beyond input-format conversion and introduce a knowledge-extraction method designed by us. Its downstream performance would make the respective contributions of Resource2Skill and the added extraction procedure difficult to distinguish. Given these differences in knowledge objectives and the adaptation requirements of the released implementation, we did not include Resource2Skill as an original-pipeline baseline alongside VisualSkill and SkillFoundry under the same evaluation setting.

Appendix P Supplementary Evaluation of Frontier Models

We additionally evaluate Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra on ScienceBoard-Verified, both with the xhigh reasoning setting. Claude Opus 5.5 shows comparatively limited computer-use performance in this scientific-software evaluation, so we do not further evaluate it with Skills and References in this supplementary study. GPT-6 Astra demonstrates substantially stronger performance. We therefore evaluate it with ScienceCUA’s self-evolved Skills and References to examine whether a stronger base model can still benefit from external operational knowledge.

As shown in Figure 11, adding ScienceCUA’s self-evolved library increases GPT-6 Astra’s average success rate from 75.19% to 77.30%, a gain of 2.11 percentage points. These results show that the self-evolved library still provides a modest additional benefit on this stronger base model, supporting the discussion in Appendix A.
